title: How To Improve Reading Scores
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Stepping outside his usual classroom-management focus, Linsin lays out three changes he'd make immediately to address historically low national reading scores. First, phonics-only instruction for 60 minutes a day in kindergarten and first grade, explicitly separated from 'balanced literacy' approaches that mix in sight words and context clues, which he argues confuses students and delays decoding mastery; older struggling readers should similarly step back into intensive phonics before rejoining grade-level content. Second, building a schoolwide culture of pleasure reading through daily teacher read-alouds chosen for adventure and drama rather than discussion-worthy social themes, plus extended daily independent reading time, arguing that reading volume correlates with success across every academic subject, even math. Third, restoring grammar instruction (parts of speech, sentence diagramming) as a foundation for comprehension, vocabulary, and writing, arguing it's a building block too often abandoned as old-fashioned. He closes with a call to remove phones from the school day entirely, arguing they actively undermine both learning to read and developing a love of reading.
points: Teach phonics-only for 60 minutes daily in K-1, explicitly separated from 'balanced literacy' methods mixing in sight words and context clues, which he argues confuses students and delays decoding.
Older students behind in reading, at any grade, should step back into an intensive systematic phonics program via testing rather than muddling through grade-level text.
Build a culture of pleasure reading through daily teacher read-alouds chosen for adventure, drama, and wonder rather than discussion-driven social topics, plus extended independent reading time.
Reading volume correlates with success across every academic subject, even math, because students can't adequately engage with content they can't read at grade level.
Restore grammar instruction (parts of speech, sentence diagramming) as a foundation for comprehension, vocabulary, and writing rather than treating it as old-fashioned.
Remove phones from the entire school day, including transitions and breaks, arguing they actively undermine both learning to read and developing a love of reading.
quotes: For context, reading scores are the lowest they’ve been in decades. Just 33 percent of fourth graders and 31 percent of eighth graders are proficient.
The teaching of sight words, pictures, context, and other clues in the early grades confuses students and subverts the mastering of phonetic skills.
Thus, kindergarten and first grade teachers must focus on phonics-only instruction for 60 minutes per day baseline, while eschewing any and all other learning-to-read methods.

The focus of read-aloud shouldn’t be on discussion-inducing topics, social issues, news articles, or cross-teaching of other academic subjects—which is de rigueur in schools today—but rather on what captivates young readers.
Because students who read more do better in every academic measure. The number of words read per day strongly correlates with school success—even math.
Knowing the parts of speech and diagramming sentences seems old fashioned, I get it. But it develops a deep appreciation for language and its inherent beauty.
Phones should be put away for the entire day, even during transitions and between-class breaks and walking periods. They impede both learning to read and developing a love of reading.
